rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites think their addressees will not believe them without oaths; decent, dignified people trust their character and have no need to swear.
rows.anchor: People who are decent and dignified have confidence in their character and therefore do not have any need to swear oaths.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘A familiar obedience’ may be an indefinite qualified subject with an omitted predicate, or a predicate with an omitted subject; either construction foregrounds the expressed words.
rows.anchor: these words form an inchoative ( mubtadā’) of a suppressed enunciative ( khabar)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Messenger has clearly delivered God’s religion to the hypocrites; making them accept it is not his duty, and they will answer to God for their response.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) has fulfilled his responsibility of delivering God’s religion to them with clarity.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that obedience to the Messenger brings guidance is both assurance of success and warning that refusal makes them responsible for their own ruin.
rows.anchor: The words “And if you obey him alone, you will be guided” sound warning as well as assurance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Messenger’s precise obligation is to communicate the message clearly; failure by his audience to respond leaves them to bear its consequences.
rows.anchor: the responsibility of the Messenger is only to clearly communicate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True faith requires obedience to God through obedience to the Messenger, not verbal profession: hypocrites professed and pledged faith too, and 4:145 places them in Hell’s lowest level.
rows.anchor: the essential consequence of faith is showing obedience to God and His Messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise of authority and security answers hypocrites’ doubts about Islam’s future; its fulfillment is also detailed in al-Anbiyā’, al-Ḥajj, and al-Mu’minūn.
rows.anchor: This verse addresses the doubt harboured by the hypocrites regarding the future of Islam.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Those before them’ means earlier messengers and their nations: after conclusive delivery, messengers and followers triumph, deniers are destroyed, and leadership passes to believers.
rows.anchor: The words “the way He had granted it to those before them” refer to the earlier messengers and their nations.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chosen religion is Islam, as in 5:6; establishing it means enforcing its law and basing the collective and political order on it.
rows.anchor: The words “He shall establish this religion that He has chosen for them” refer to the religion of Islam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers’ fear and uncertainty are temporary: God will make the land secure, so no one will dare threaten His religion or its bearers there.
rows.anchor: The words “after this state of their fear, He shall transform it into peace” are very meaningful

rows.speaker: the Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: After the conquest of Makkah, the promise was fulfilled across Arabia; the Prophet said that two religions would not coexist there.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) said: ﻵﻹ ﻳﺠﺘﻤﻊ ﻓﻴﻬﺎ دﻳﻨﺎن two religions will never simultaneously exist here

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those still opposing God’s religion are being tested and given respite; a verdict will soon fall on those disobedient to God and His Messenger, bringing humiliation.
rows.anchor: those who are opposing God’s religion are being given respite because they are passing through the period of test and trial ordained for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing clause identifies the consequence of the opponents’ disobedience.
rows.anchor: The purpose of the last part of the sentence is to refer to its consequence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s chapter structure pairs sūrahs; al-Aḥzāb summarizes and supplements its chapter, like al-Nūr does for the preceding chapter.
rows.anchor: The principle of sūrahs occurring in pairs can be witnessed in this chapter also

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Across the chapter are the phases of Muhammad’s mission—warning, migration, and war—and the core themes of monotheism, prophethood, and the Hereafter; its reasoning style is distinct.
rows.anchor: All phases of the preaching mission of Prophet Muḥammad (sws) – warning, migration and war – as well as all basic topics as monotheism, prophethood and the hereafter are also discussed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chapter’s comprehensive theme is affirming prophethood: it answers Quraysh and allies on Muhammad’s prophethood and the Qur’an’s divinity, explains their true status, promises believers reward after trial, and warns persistent deniers after conclusive proof.
rows.anchor: The comprehensive theme of this sūrah is affirmation of prophethood.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Furqān defends the Qur’an and Prophet by answering opponents’ objections, alluding to their motives, and arguing further on issues they resist, including monotheism and punishment.
rows.anchor: The theme of this sūrah is to defend the Qur’ ān and the Prophet (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In verses 1–9, the Qur’an is a blessed, merciful revelation, yet deniers of monotheism and the Hereafter call it a fabrication and conspiracy.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ ān has been revealed by the most blessed being as the most blessed and merciful thing.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening passage points to opponents’ propaganda intended to turn people away from the Prophet and the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: A reference is made to the propaganda worked by the opponents of the Prophet (sws) to lead people away from him and the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction corresponding to the earlier Qur’anic phrase conveys firm decision and strong will.
rows.anchor: This style expresses a certain decision and a strong will.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mention of reciting revelations to the people of Madyan alludes to Shuʿayb’s story; Muhammad was not deputed to warn them but was informed of their circumstances, proving he had the same mission as earlier messengers.
rows.anchor: the anecdote of Shu‘ayb (sws) which has been mentioned in many sūrahs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad was absent when God called Moses at Ṭūr; he knew these events only through God’s mercy in making him a messenger, clear evidence of his prophethood.
rows.anchor: For this reason, all these events were brought to his knowledge.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before “as a mercy,” the verb “We sent you” is understood but omitted.
rows.anchor: a verb to the effect أَرْﺳَﻠْﻨَﺎكَ is suppressed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unwarned nation is the Ishmaelites: they lacked familiarity with God’s Book and law, had received no earlier messenger, and Muhammad was sent from among them in answer to Abraham’s prayer.
rows.anchor: This is a reference to the Ishmaelites.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning is a great mercy if valued, but becomes a calamity if rejected; God’s established practice is to destroy a people that does not reform after a messenger warns it.
rows.anchor: The established practice of God is that if

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author compares Muhammad’s mission to Quraysh with Moses’s mission to Pharaoh and calls it a boon if valued.
rows.anchor: a great boon if they gave regard to it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Failing to value Muhammad’s messengership would turn it into a bane.
rows.anchor: great bane if they did not value it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mission concludes the truth for Quraysh, so they cannot claim ignorance if punishment comes after the warning.
rows.anchor: the truth conclusively to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jews taught Quraysh to object that Muhammad lacked miracles like Moses; the response asks whether Moses’s own people ever took those miracles seriously.
rows.anchor: regard these miracles with seriousness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People of the Book who support the Qur’an in light of prophecies in their scriptures are praised for enduring their people’s uproar.
rows.anchor: prophecies mentioned in their scriptures

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh fear that following the message would expel them from their homeland is answered with reassurance of safety if they accept; rejection will bring destruction under God’s established practice.
rows.anchor: be uprooted from the land.

none: The segment contains verse translations only and adds no commentary to record.
